content: Type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM), previously referred to as non-insulin-dependent diabetes mellitus (NIDDM), obesity-related diabetes, or adult-onset diabetes, is a metabolic disorder primarily characterized by insulin resistance, relative insulin deficiency, and hyperglycemia. The impaired responsiveness of body tissues to insulin is believed to involve defects in the insulin receptor located on cell membranes. In the early stages of the disease, the predominant abnormality is reduced insulin sensitivity, which is often accompanied by elevated levels of insulin in the blood. At this stage, hyperglycemia can often be managed through lifestyle interventions such as exercise, dietary modifications, and medications that enhance insulin sensitivity or reduce hepatic glucose production. However, as the disease progresses, insulin secretion becomes increasingly impaired, often necessitating therapeutic insulin replacement. The prevalence of T2DM is rapidly increasing in developed countries, and there is evidence to suggest that this trend will extend to other parts of the world in the coming years. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) has described this rise as an epidemic. Diabetes mellitus has been recognized as a disease since ancient times. In 1812, it was formally identified as a clinical entity in the New England Journal of Medicine and Surgery. By 1889, the pancreas was identified as playing a central role in the disease's pathogenesis. The discovery of insulin in 1921 by Frederick Banting and Charles Best marked a significant milestone in diabetes management, as they successfully reversed the diabetic state in dogs by injecting pancreatic extracts from healthy animals. Type 2 diabetes does not have a specific classification system, but diabetes mellitus as a whole is categorized into three main types: Type 1 diabetes mellitus (T1DM), Type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM), and gestational diabetes. The pathophysiology of T2DM is rooted in the development of insulin resistance. Unlike T1DM, individuals with T2DM produce sufficient insulin, but their cells exhibit a diminished response to circulating insulin. The mechanisms underlying insulin resistance are thought to be influenced by both genetic and environmental factors. Environmental contributors include high-glycemic diets, central obesity, advanced age, male gender, low-fiber diets, and diets high in saturated fats. The primary cause of T2DM is insulin resistance, although the exact mechanisms remain unclear. Central obesity, aging, and high-glycemic diets are the most commonly implicated factors in the development of the disease. T2DM must be differentiated from other conditions that may present with similar symptoms, such as polyuria, polydipsia, weight loss, or weight gain. For example, glucocorticoid use or certain medical conditions can mimic these symptoms. The prevalence of T2DM has been extensively studied in developed countries, but there is significant variability in data from developing nations, particularly in rural areas with limited access to healthcare. Globally, it is estimated that approximately 50% of adults with diabetes remain undiagnosed. In the United States, African Americans, Mexican Americans, American Indians, and non-Hispanic Blacks are at higher risk of developing T2DM compared to non-Hispanic Whites. The disease is more common in individuals over the age of 65, although there is a growing trend of childhood-onset T2DM. In 2011, an estimated 335 million people worldwide had T2DM, and this number is projected to exceed 500 million by 2050. The prevalence rates correspond to approximately 5,000 per 100,000 in 2011 and 7,500 per 100,000 by 2050. T2DM is more prevalent in men than women and is more common in lowto middle-income countries compared to high-income nations. It is classified as a global epidemic, growing in parallel with rapid urbanization. Screening for diabetes is recommended for individuals at various life stages and for those with specific risk factors. The same tests used for diagnosis are employed for screening. Early diagnosis and treatment can help control complications and lead to better clinical outcomes. If left untreated, T2DM can result in acute complications such as hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state (HHS) and, in rare cases, diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA). Chronic complications include microvascular and macrovascular damage. Early diagnosis and prompt treatment of these complications can improve prognosis and reduce long-term morbidity and mortality. A detailed medical history is essential for individuals presenting with symptoms of diabetes. Classic symptoms include weight loss, polyphagia, polydipsia, and polyuria. Less common symptoms may include vision changes, tingling or numbness in the extremities, fatigue, and skin changes. Physical examination findings are often normal unless complications have developed. Common findings may include pigmented skin patches and acanthosis nigricans. Laboratory findings are diagnostic for T2DM. The disease can be diagnosed using plasma glucose criteria, including fasting plasma glucose (FPG), the 2-hour plasma glucose (2-h PG) value after a 75-g oral glucose tolerance test (OGTT), or hemoglobin A1c (HbA1c) levels. All these measurements are equally valid for diagnosis. Lifestyle modification is a cornerstone of diabetes management and includes diabetes self-management education (DSME), diabetes self-management support (DSMS), nutrition therapy, physical activity, smoking cessation counseling, and psychosocial care. The goals of DSME and DSMS are to support informed decision-making, self-care behaviors, problem-solving, and active collaboration with the healthcare team to improve clinical outcomes, health status, and quality of life in a cost-effective manner. Medical therapy aims to eliminate hyperglycemic symptoms, control long-term complications, and improve the patient’s quality of life. T2DM is initially managed with lifestyle changes and weight loss, particularly in obese patients. Metformin is the first-line pharmacologic therapy unless contraindications exist. If glycemic goals are not achieved, a second agent is added to metformin. A variety of options are available for combination therapy, tailored to the patient’s condition and comorbidities. Dual therapy is initiated in cases where HbA1c is greater than 9%. For patients with HbA1c levels exceeding 10%, blood glucose levels above 300 mg/dL, or those with significant symptoms, combination therapy with insulin is considered. Pancreas and islet cell transplantation may be considered for patients with chronic diabetes who experience frequent metabolic complications, are intolerant to exogenous insulin, or have failed insulin therapy. Primary prevention of T2DM focuses on lifestyle modification. Metformin may also be used as an adjunctive measure in high-risk individuals. Studies have shown that a 7% weight loss within six months in obese individuals is effective in preventing diabetes. Secondary prevention strategies aim to reduce macrovascular complications. Lipid control, smoking cessation, and treatment of hypertension are critical secondary preventive measures.
